results.content: [Activism](https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/tag/activism/), [AI](https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/tag/ai/), [Board of Directors](https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/tag/board-of-directors/), [Corporate governance](https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/tag/corporate-governance/). [Rich Fields](https://www.russellreynolds.com/en/people/consultant-directory/rich-fields)leads the Board Effectiveness Practice,Melissa Martin is a member of the Board Effectiveness Practice, and[Rusty O’Kelley](https://www.russellreynolds.com/en/people/consultant-directory/jack-rusty-okelley) is a Managing Director at Russell Reynolds Associates. Across the globe, boards are increasingly expected to demonstrate baseline[AI literacy](https://www.russellreynolds.com/en/insights/articles/leaders-views-on-generative-ai-in-2025)to capitalize on the significant opportunities while avoiding or mitigating material risks. But even where the legal environment is less prescriptive,[boards are enhancing their own capabilities](https://www.russellreynolds.com/en/insights/articles/the-new-qualified-technology-executive), from adding AI-related experience as a target for director recruiting to providing more comprehensive education and training for their directors. Across markets, board and individual director evaluations are becoming more rigorous and more frequent, with increasing use of external facilitators and a shift away from purely collegial, high-level reviews in Brazil, Italy, and Singapore, much like we have[previously noted in the United States](https://www.russellreynolds.com/en/insights/reports-surveys/2022-global-and-regional-trends-in-corporate-governance).
